title: {{NAME}} and the Princess Who Spoke to Wolves
moral: Understanding someone different from yourself begins with the willingness to truly listen.

pages.content:
The kingdom of Arvenwood was the kind of place where the trees grew tall enough to hold clouds, and the palace at its centre glittered like a crown someone had left on a hilltop and forgotten. {{NAME}} had arrived there by way of a market cart and a wrong turn, which, as it happened, was the best possible way to arrive anywhere interesting.

The trouble with Arvenwood that morning was unmistakable even from the palace gates. The wolves had come to the treeline. Not lurking. Not threatening. They sat in a perfectly straight line at the forest's edge, all twelve of them, staring at the palace with an expression that on a human face would have been called desperate.

Every guard had their hand on a spear. Every courtier had gone pale. And in the centre of it all, standing alone between the palace steps and the treeline with her arms crossed and her chin up, was a girl in a moss-green gown embroidered with silver leaves. Princess Mira. She was not afraid. She was furious.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} slipped past two arguing guards and made his way to where Princess Mira stood. Up close she was about his age, with a sharp, quick face and ink-stained fingers that suggested she spent more time in the library than at royal banquets.

'Do you know what they're saying?' he asked, nodding toward the wolves.

Mira turned and looked at him with the kind of look that measures a person very thoroughly in one second flat. 'I'm trying to,' she said. 'I've studied the old wolf-language but it's mostly used for weather and territory. Whatever this is, it's something they don't have words for yet.'

{{NAME}}'s eyes went wide. The lead wolf, enormous and silver-grey, had risen to its feet. It was looking directly at Mira with an expression he understood completely, the look of someone trying to say something important in a language with gaps in all the wrong places.

'They need help,' {{NAME}} said quietly. He was very certain of it, the way you are certain of things that have always been true.

pages.content:
Mira did something then that no princess in Arvenwood's long history had ever done: she walked forward. Not slowly, not tentatively. She walked toward the wolves with the purposeful stride of someone who had made up her mind and was not interested in changing it.

{{NAME}} walked beside her. The guards behind them were shouting. Neither of them looked back.

The silver wolf lowered its great head as they approached. Behind it the pack shifted and parted to reveal a narrow path leading into the forest, and at the end of that path, visible even from here, a terrible sight: the great oak at the heart of the wolves' territory had fallen across a den entrance, trapping something inside. Something small. Something that made tiny frantic sounds whenever the wind went quiet.

Mira dropped to her knees in the leaves, pressed her ear to the gap, and listened. Then she looked up at {{NAME}} with a completely different expression. Gone was the fury. What replaced it was raw, unguarded feeling.

'Cubs,' she said. 'Three of them. They've been trying to tell us for two days.'

pages.content:
Moving the oak took every set of hands from the palace: guards, courtiers, even the cook. Mira organised them with precise instructions while {{NAME}} worked beside the silver wolf, both of them pushing at the same enormous branch, and the wolf leaned its great weight against his shoulder as though they had been doing this kind of work together for years.

It took an hour. It took splinters and sweat and three broken tool handles. But when the last section rolled clear, three small bundles of grey fur tumbled out of the den into the afternoon light, blinking enormously and immediately climbing over each other in a chaos of small paws and ecstatic yipping.

The silver wolf made a sound unlike anything {{NAME}} had ever heard, low and resonant and trembling, the kind of sound that bypasses the ears and goes straight to somewhere deeper. The whole pack pressed together around the cubs.

Mira sat back in the leaves and put her hands over her face. When she lowered them, she was smiling in the slightly embarrassed way of people who did not expect to feel as much as they do.

pages.content:
That evening, the wolves did not return to the deep forest. They settled at the treeline in a loose, comfortable sprawl, the cubs rolling over each other in the last of the light. The palace gates stayed open.

Mira sat beside {{NAME}} on the palace steps with a bowl of honey bread between them and a stack of her wolf-language notes in her lap. She was adding new words that did not exist in any book yet, words she had learned today. The silver wolf lay at the foot of the steps with one huge grey chin resting on its paws, watching the cubs with a slow, satisfied gaze.

{{NAME}} leaned back on his hands and looked up at the cloud-tall trees, then at the stars beginning to appear above them. The castle had felt like a cold and complicated place this morning. It felt entirely different now.

His eyes grew warm and slow. One of the small cubs had waddled over and fallen asleep against his boot, all tiny heaving sides and velvet ears.

Goodnight, brave visitor. Sleep well, and wonder what new words Mira might teach the wolves tomorrow.
